title: GPU adjacency-reset synthesis & tactical runbook (draft)
content:
Summary:

A recurring class of instability observed in a subset of our GPU nodes where a rapid sequence of link resets (PCIe / NVLink adjacency resets) precedes either a correctable ECC spike or a full driver hang. This doc captures the most recent incident cluster (Apr–Jun 2028), hypotheses, short-term mitigations we have tried, and a concise tactical runbook for oncall to gather safe diagnostics and perform recovery with minimal customer impact.

Why this matters:
- Affected workloads: long-context batch inference and quantized-model low-latency chat tasks; we see highest failure rates on nodes running 80GB A100-like instances with dense NVSwitch topologies.
- End-user impact: transient errors returned to hosts, occasional long-running RPC timeouts leading to failed requests and client-visible latency spikes.
- Business impact: elevated token-err rates for production tenants on Dedicated pools; risk of cross-tenant retries.

Incident pattern (synthesis of multiple traces):
- t0: small increase in NVLink correctable counters (nvlink_err_count ~ +30/min) reported by telemetry sampler.
- t0+2m: PCIe slot adjacencies show link-training events (dmesg shows "link training retry") across 2–4 GPUs in the node.
- t0+3–5m: GPU driver reports CORRECTABLE ECC bursts (nvidia-smi ecc errors), then a single GPU stops responding to NVML calls.
- t0+6–10m: kernel oops or driver hang observed; pod eviction or container restart follows.
- Recovery: soft-reboot or full node reboot resolves for 6–72 hours.

Key telemetry signals to watch (what helped detect these incidents):
- nvlink.err_cor_cnt (per-GPU time-series)
- pci.link_retrain_count (host-level sysfs metric)
- nvidia_driver_uptime / nvml_timeout_count
- pod_restart_rate and rpc_timeout_95th per model-route
- dmesg kernel messages containing "link training", "AER", "GPU hung"
- temperature and VRM sensors (to rule out thermal triggers)

Evidence collected (Apr–Jun cluster):
- Kernel logs (attached in SRE-4572) show repeated link retraining followed by AER reports referencing lanes in the backplane.
- Hardware scrapings: two chassis with adjacent PCIe risers showed higher ECC counts on the GPUs nearest the riser connectors.
- Driver stacktraces show nv-peer-memory calls blocked on nvlink workqueue after a retrain event.
- No single firmware/cable vendor correlation strong enough yet, but higher prevalence in chassis with older backplane firmware (v1.3.2).

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Intermittent link-training failures due to marginal signal integrity on specific backplane channels, exacerbated by high NVLink utilization and aggressive power management.
2) Firmware mismatch between NVSwitch/backplane and host SMC leading to occasional negotiation regressions under bursty traffic.
3) Driver-level bug causing workqueue starvation after a retrain event (less likely given hardware evidence).

Short-term mitigations tried and current status:
- Conservative: set nvlink_agg_policy=low on affected node pools — reduced incident rate by ~40% but increased per-token latency slightly.
- Firmware roll-forward on two suspect chassis to v1.3.5 — one chassis showed no recurrences in 10 days, other unchanged.
- Driver rollback to earlier stable driver on an isolated pool — correlated drop in driver-hang reports but not in ECC bursts.
- Pod scheduling tweak: add anti-affinity to avoid placing adjacent heavy-NVLink workloads together — operationally noisy and reduces utilization.

Tactical runbook (for oncall):
Purpose: capture safe diagnostic data, stabilize serving, and restore capacity with minimal customer impact.
Preconditions: before touching nodes, check active customer jobs + scheduled infra maintenance windows.

1) Detecting an event (alert triggers):
- Alert conditions: nvlink.err_cor_cnt > 20/min on any GPU OR driver_hang_count > 0
- On alert, gather quick-snapshot:
  - /usr/local/bin/tele-snapshot.sh --gpus --dmesg --nvlink --sysfs > /tmp/gpu-snap-$(date +%s).log
  - Query: curl -s "$TELEMETRY_API/series?metric=nvlink.err_cor_cnt&host=$NODE"
- Post initial snapshot to slack thread (#sre-oncall) and attach to JIRA SRE-4572.

2) Immediate triage: (non-invasive)
- Check temperatures: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=temperature.gpu --format=csv,noheader
- Check ECC counters: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=ecc.error.corrected.volatile --format=csv,noheader
- Inspect dmesg for link retrain and AER messages: dmesg | egrep -i "link training|AER|GPU hung|nvlink"
- If driver responding: nvmlDeviceGetNVLinkBandwidthSample or nvlink-cli to check link state.

3) Safe containment steps (if multiple GPUs in node show errors):
- Move vulnerable pods off the node using cordon + evict with graceful period: kubectl cordon $NODE; kubectl drain $NODE --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120
  - If draining would cause customer SLA breach, optionally schedule manual pod relocation for highest priority tenants only.
- If node already non-responsive to kubectl and remote SSH unavailable, escalate to SRE senior for platform-level reboot.

4) Recovery options (ordered by preference):
- Option A (preferred): perform a soft driver unload/reload and re-run health checks: 
  - sudo systemctl stop redwood-agent && sudo rmmod nvidia_uvm nvidia && sudo modprobe nvidia && sudo systemctl start redwood-agent
  - Note: this is NOT safe if kernel stack traces indicate oops — prefer full node reboot if kernel panics are present.
- Option B (when soft reload fails): schedule a full node reboot through standard maintenance pipeline and revalidate telemetry post-boot.
- Option C (when recurring on same chassis): place chassis into Quarantine pool (tag nodes) and schedule hardware swap/inspection.

5) Data to collect for postmortem (must complete before node rejoins pool):
- full dmesg and kernel ring buffer (dmesg -T)
- nvlink sysfs snapshots: for g in /sys/class/nvlink/*; do cat $g/*; done
- lspci -vvv for adapter lanes
- nvidia-smi -q -x > nvidia-snap.xml
- SMM logs from baseboard (if available) and BMC event log
- Telemetry traces (5–10 minutes pre and post event) exported to S3 and linked in ticket.

6) Follow-ups and permanent mitigations to prioritize (post-incident):
- Run controlled stress test across chassis with older backplane firmware to reproduce link retrain under load (assigned: Marco N., ETA 3w).
- Expand per-node nvlink sampling rate to 10s for suspect pools to improve signal-to-noise for heuristic detectors (assigned: Lina O., ETA 2w).
- Draft a firmware upgrade schedule and vendor engagement plan (assigned: Hardware Eng).
- Prototype automatic soft-fallback policy in routing layer: if a node starts showing link retrains escalate routing to capacity-tiered fallback models.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Why some chassis respond to firmware roll-forward while others do not? Could be a subtle hardware revision difference. Need vendor trace logs.
- Is there an intermittent maintenance window in some colo racks causing power rails shifts (suspect after correlating with BMC logs)?

Runbook cautions / gotchas:
- DO NOT attempt rmmod nvidia if kernel oops involving GPU stacks are present; doing so can hang the host and require manual intervention.
- Soft unloads can hide underlying hardware flakiness; only use as temporary recovery, not long-term fix.
- Reboots will disrupt in-flight long-context streaming sessions—communicate with CS for high-impact customers.

Appendix A — quick commands cheat-sheet:
- tele-snapshot (internal): /usr/local/bin/tele-snapshot.sh --gpus --dmesg --nvlink --sysfs 
- ECC counters: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=ecc.error.corrected.volatile --format=csv,noheader
- NVLink sysfs dump: for g in /sys/class/nvlink/*; do echo $g; cat $g/*; done > /tmp/nvlink-snapshot.txt
- driver stack: sudo journalctl -u nvidia-driver.service -n 500 | sed -n '1,400p'

Appendix B — related tickets and notes:
- JIRA SRE-4572: cluster trace + dmesg archives (incidents Apr 18, May 9, Jun 11)
- GH PR #189: telemetry sampler upgrade to include pci.link_retrain_count
- Confluence: gpu-adj-reset-playbook (working doc, contains vendor comms)

Last notes: this doc is intentionally terse and pragmatic—aim is to help any oncaller quickly identify the adjacency-reset pattern, collect the right evidence, and stabilize capacity. Please append additional reproducible artifacts and vendor traces here as we get them.

-- Aisha P. (oncall lead)
